title: Camelcase Matching
description: Brute force to optimized: branching over insertion choices versus a single greedy two-pointer pass.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array of query strings and a pattern string, a query matches the pattern if a sequence of lowercase letters can be inserted (possibly none) at any positions in pattern to make it equal to the query. Return a boolean array indicating which queries match.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","queries array, pattern string"],["Output","Boolean array, true where inserting only lowercase letters into pattern can produce the query"],["Key Insight","Every uppercase letter in the query MUST appear in pattern, in the same relative order; lowercase letters can be freely inserted anywhere"],["Constraints","Up to 100 queries and pattern length up to 100"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Insert lowercase letters to transform pattern into query\"","A two-pointer greedy walk: consume query characters one at a time, only requiring the pattern pointer to advance on a match"],["\"Uppercase letters are special (camelCase boundaries)\"","Any uppercase letter in the query that fails to match the current pattern character immediately disqualifies the query"]]}

blocks.text: Walking through the query character by character with a separate pointer into pattern: whenever the query character equals the current pattern character, advance both pointers (consuming a "kept" letter). Otherwise, if the query character is lowercase, it is simply an inserted letter, skip it (advance only the query pointer). But if the query character is UPPERCASE and does not match, the query cannot possibly be formed this way, since uppercase letters can never be "inserted", only kept from pattern.

blocks.title: Analogy: Checking If a Word Could Have Been Abbreviated
blocks.text: Picture checking if a full compound word could have been abbreviated down to a shorter capitalized code by only ever dropping lowercase letters. Any uppercase letter in the full word must appear, in order, within the abbreviation; any lowercase letter can be freely dropped without consequence.

blocks.caption: Lowercase query letters can be freely skipped; uppercase query letters must match the next pattern character

blocks.text: Result: [true,false,true,true,false]. "FooBar" matches (F, then oo skipped, B, then ar skipped, fully consuming pattern "FB"). "FooBarTest" fails since after consuming "FB" fully, the remaining uppercase "T" in "Test" has no more pattern characters to match. "FrameBuffer" matches similarly to "FooBar".

Before trying every possible way to insert lowercase letters into pattern (an exponential search), notice that since insertions can ONLY be lowercase letters, a single greedy left-to-right walk suffices: there is never a choice to make, since an uppercase query letter has exactly one valid interpretation (it must match the current pattern character) and a lowercase one has exactly one valid interpretation too (it is always safe to treat as inserted, UNLESS greedily matching it against pattern would be needed, which the greedy match-when-equal rule naturally handles).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The only characters that can be freely inserted into pattern to form the query are LOWERCASE letters; pattern's own characters (which may include uppercase or lowercase) must all appear in the query, in order.

Observation 2: Walking the query left to right with a pattern pointer, whenever the current query character equals the current pattern character, it is safe (and necessary, to keep pace) to advance the pattern pointer too.

Observation 3: If the query character does not match the current pattern character, it can only be a valid insertion if it is lowercase; if it is uppercase, the query is impossible to form.

Observation 4: The query matches overall if and only if, after processing every query character this way, the pattern pointer has advanced all the way to the end of pattern (every pattern character was successfully matched).

This leads to a single-pass two-pointer greedy walk per query: advance the pattern pointer on a match, reject immediately on an unmatched uppercase letter, and check the pattern pointer reached the end.
Conceptually, try every possible subsequence-based way of inserting lowercase letters into pattern and check if any produces the exact query string.
Why the code is written this way

items: Branching at every character to try both interpretations implements the definition directly.

This branching is unnecessary: matching greedily whenever possible is always at least as good as skipping, since pattern must be matched in order and skipping a matchable character can only delay progress.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(2 raised to the query length) worst case for the branching backtrack.
Space: O(query length) recursion depth.
Limitation: a single greedy two-pointer pass removes the branching entirely, since the correct choice at each character is always determined.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Walk query with a pointer i and track a separate pattern pointer starting at 0. For each character in query: if the pattern pointer is not past the end AND the query character equals pattern at the pattern pointer, advance the pattern pointer (a kept, matched character). Otherwise, if the query character is uppercase, the query cannot match, return false immediately. Otherwise (lowercase, unmatched), simply continue (it is a valid insertion). After the full walk, the query matches if and only if the pattern pointer reached the end of pattern.
Greedily match query characters against pattern in one linear pass; uppercase mismatches immediately disqualify the query.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Query char","Pattern pointer before","Action"],"rows":[["F","0 (F)","Matches, advance pattern pointer to 1"],["o","1 (B)","Lowercase, does not match B, skip (insertion)"],["o","1 (B)","Same, skip"],["B","1 (B)","Matches, advance pattern pointer to 2 (end)"],["a, r","2 (end)","Both lowercase, skip; pattern pointer already at end, MATCH"]]}

blocks.text: Since only lowercase letters may be freely inserted, matching greedily whenever the current query character equals the current pattern character is always correct: there is never a benefit to skipping a matchable character, since pattern's remaining characters must still all be matched later in the same order regardless. Any uppercase character that fails to match immediately proves the query is impossible, since it cannot have been inserted.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(total characters across all queries).
Space: O(1) extra per query beyond the output array.

blocks.text: Camelcase Matching is a clean greedy two-pointer problem once the key rule is spotted: uppercase letters are non-negotiable, lowercase letters are always safely skippable when unmatched.

items: Treating this as requiring backtracking or dynamic programming when a single greedy pass is fully sufficient and provably correct.
Forgetting to check that the pattern pointer reached the very END of pattern, not just that no mismatch occurred.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["Query equals pattern exactly","Matches trivially."],["Query is missing an uppercase letter present in pattern","Never matches, the pattern pointer cannot reach the end."]]}

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "uppercase must match, lowercase can always be skipped, so there is never an actual choice to make" justifies why a greedy single pass (no backtracking) is provably correct.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "insert lowercase letters to transform one string into another", think: a greedy two-pointer walk where only uppercase mismatches are fatal.

items: How would this change if BOTH uppercase and lowercase letters could be freely inserted (a simple subsequence check)?
Is Subsequence, a closely related two-pointer greedy matching problem.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The branching backtrack approach costs O(2^query length) worst case; the greedy two-pointer approach costs O(total characters), the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: greedy two-pointer matching with a special rule for uppercase characters.
Core Idea: uppercase query letters must match pattern exactly and in order; lowercase letters can always be treated as free insertions when unmatched.
Time: O(2^query length) worst case for the brute force, O(total characters) for the greedy approach.
Space: O(query length) recursion depth for the brute force, O(1) extra for the greedy approach.
Most Important Observation: there is never an actual branching decision, the greedy match-when-possible rule is always correct.
Interview Difficulty: a clean, quick greedy two-pointer problem.
One line memory trick: uppercase must match, lowercase always slides through.
